value.title: How I Wrote UI Tests for the Get Hacking Android App

content.subtitle: The Android team and community advocates testing. This includes unit, integration, and UI testing.

paragraphs.name: e8fe
paragraphs.text: How I Wrote UI Tests for the Get Hacking Android App

paragraphs.name: e334
paragraphs.text: Editor’s note: Zhao Wei interned with us from January to March 2019, before beginning his Full-Time National Service obligations. He worked on an impressive variety of software and hardware projects, including web apps, chatbots, native apps, and more. Here, he goes into a deep dive on what he learned about Android UI testing:

paragraphs.name: a44d
paragraphs.text: The Android team and community advocates testing. This includes unit, integration, and UI testing.

paragraphs.name: 99ce
paragraphs.text: I’ll focus on UI testing for this post.

paragraphs.name: c511
paragraphs.text: Testing brings about several benefits to the app development process:

paragraphs.name: ea05
paragraphs.text: Acts as a specification for the app’s behaviour

paragraphs.name: aa16
paragraphs.text: Verifies that the app behaves according to the specification

paragraphs.name: d25e
paragraphs.text: Gives confidence that any changes made during development do not break existing functionality

paragraphs.name: b12b
paragraphs.text: The last point is especially important to apps undergoing major refactors and redesigns. Get Hacking Android is no exception.

paragraphs.name: a423
paragraphs.text: The Initial State of Get Hacking Android

paragraphs.name: 74cb
paragraphs.text:
Get Hacking - Digital Maker - Apps on Google Play
Get Hacking with the micro:bit! Browse our collection of electronics projects, powered by the micro:bit, and start your…play.google.com

paragraphs.name: 03cf
paragraphs.text: Get Hacking Android is an app that showcases micro:bit and maker projects. Tinkertanker released a first version over a year ago on the Play Store, but without any UI tests for the app. This meant that functionality could break during development without anyone noticing. (Unfortunately, some of these bugs did actually slip into production.)

paragraphs.name: ff30
paragraphs.text: The app is also undergoing a major redesign, and this impacts many areas of the code base. Breakages are likely to happen.
Writing UI tests can help avoid these issues. I’ve written some and documented what I’ve learnt below. This includes some of the patterns I’ve followed and the pitfalls I’ve encountered.

paragraphs.name: 65de
paragraphs.text: Preparing to Test

paragraphs.name: f943
paragraphs.text: Before writing any tests, I set up the dependencies needed for testing. These include the Espresso and AndroidX Test libraries.

paragraphs.name: 7b3b
paragraphs.text: The Espresso and AndroidX Test dependencies used in Get Hacking Android

paragraphs.name: af9e
paragraphs.text: What Is Espresso?

paragraphs.name: cba1
paragraphs.text: Espresso is a UI testing library for Android. It provides APIs for writing idiomatic actions and assertions on the UI.

paragraphs.name: 4df6
paragraphs.text: The logo for Espresso

paragraphs.name: f4a5
paragraphs.text: Tests written with Espresso are concise and readable.
Look how natural Espresso code feels
What Is AndroidX Test?

paragraphs.name: 6eb5
paragraphs.text: AndroidX Test is a set of libraries to ease testing on Android. It provides test harnesses and utilities that make writing tests simpler.
The logo for AndroidX Test
The JUnit and Truth extensions provide methods for fluent assertions. These exist under the androidx.test.ext namespace.

paragraphs.name: c116
paragraphs.text: AndroidJUnitRunner makes it possible to run JUnit-style tests on Android devices. It exists under the androidx.test:runner namespace.

paragraphs.name: c34a
paragraphs.text: Android Test Orchestrator enhances test reliability by running tests in separate Instrumentation instances. Some of my tests were flaky and failed without it. It exists under the androidx.test:orchestrator namespace.

paragraphs.name: 58c5
paragraphs.text: Understanding the Android Test File Structure

paragraphs.name: 51aa
paragraphs.text: There are a few common rules to writing UI tests:

paragraphs.name: 5ae5
paragraphs.text: Store all on-device UI tests in the androidTest directory.

paragraphs.name: c0ea
paragraphs.text: Store each test class in the same subdirectory under androidTest as the class under test.

paragraphs.name: 8dc1
paragraphs.text: Give each test class the same name as the class under test, but suffixed with the word Test.

paragraphs.name: ffb9
paragraphs.text: Side note: Store off-device UI and unit tests in the test directory instead.

paragraphs.name: 72a6
paragraphs.text: Here’s an example.
I want to test an ExampleActivity class. I store it in app/src/main/java/com/example/example-app/ExampleActivity.java.

paragraphs.name: 04ac
paragraphs.text: In this case, I should name my test class ExampleActivityTest. I should also store it in app/src/androidTest/java/com/example/example-app/ExampleActivityTest.java.

paragraphs.name: dc82
paragraphs.text: Writing My First Test Class

paragraphs.name: 661b
paragraphs.text: To get started, I first wrote a test class for a simple Activity in the app: IntroductionActivity.

paragraphs.name: 619c
paragraphs.text: The IntroductionActivity test class

paragraphs.name: 618c
paragraphs.text: There’s a bunch of different things going on at first glance. Let’s walk through each part in more detail.

paragraphs.name: c583
paragraphs.text: Using ActivityScenario and ActivityScenarioRule

paragraphs.name: 005c
paragraphs.text: ActivityScenario is essential to testing Activities on Android. It manages the state and lifecycle events for the Activity under test. This eases Activity behaviour testing.

paragraphs.name: ab5c
paragraphs.text: ActivityScenarioRule builds upon ActivityScenario. It launches an ActivityScenario before each test and cleans up after each test.

paragraphs.name: 1ec0
paragraphs.text: For IntroductionActivityTest, I used ActivityScenarioRule to launch IntroductionActivity before each test.

paragraphs.name: b794
paragraphs.text: Writing My First Test Case

paragraphs.name: a275
paragraphs.text: The IntroductionActivity displays a TextView with introductory text and a Button.

paragraphs.name: 62b0
paragraphs.text: The first test verifies that the app displays these two views:

paragraphs.name: 04f9
paragraphs.text: The first test case for IntroductionActivityTest

paragraphs.name: 0cc6
paragraphs.text: I used Espresso APIs here. They may be unfamiliar if you haven’t written UI tests before, but the intent of the code should be clear.

paragraphs.name: 64eb
paragraphs.text: What Are These Methods?

paragraphs.name: ff9a
paragraphs.text: The Android documentation provides a detailed explanation of common Espresso APIs. For convenience, I’ll give a quick introduction to each method I used.
onView() matches a View given one or more ViewMatchers objects.

paragraphs.name: fead
paragraphs.text: check() checks the state of the matched View given one or more ViewAssertions objects.

paragraphs.name: 2beb
paragraphs.text: matches() returns a ViewAssertion object that asserts on the given ViewMatcher objects.
isDisplayed()returns a ViewMatcher object that matches a displayed View.

paragraphs.name: f316
paragraphs.text: Testing User Interactions
Clicking the Button in IntroductionActivity launches an Intent to start the MainActivity.

paragraphs.name: f281
paragraphs.text: The next test verifies this interaction.

paragraphs.name: b71d
paragraphs.text: The second test case for IntroductionActivityTest

paragraphs.name: 6caa
paragraphs.text: Naming Test Cases

paragraphs.name: 00bf
paragraphs.text: I named each test case following a structured scheme. It goes like this: [action/condition]_[expected result]().

paragraphs.name: f964
paragraphs.text: This naming scheme tells readers the intent of a test case at a glance.

paragraphs.name: f935
paragraphs.text: In onClickButton_showsMainActivity(), onClickButton is the action and showsMainActivity is the expected result.

paragraphs.name: bba4
paragraphs.text: Structuring Code in Test Cases

paragraphs.name: 48f3
paragraphs.text: The Android team recommends structuring test code based on Given-When-Then (GWT).

paragraphs.name: 27fb
paragraphs.text: GWT splits code into three phases:

paragraphs.name: a16a
paragraphs.text: Given: The initial state of the app.

paragraphs.name: fce1
paragraphs.text: When: The action to carry out. This is like the action used in naming the test case.

paragraphs.name: 3e96
paragraphs.text: Then: The expected result. This is like the expected result used in naming the test case.

paragraphs.name: 867a
paragraphs.text: In onClickButton_showsMainActivity(), I separated the three parts with a newline.

paragraphs.name: e67a
paragraphs.text: There is no Given phase in the test.

paragraphs.name: e241
paragraphs.text: onView(...) occurs during the When phase.

paragraphs.name: ee17
paragraphs.text: intended(...) occurs during the Then phase.

paragraphs.name: 7ade
paragraphs.text: Performing ViewActions

paragraphs.name: 30a0
paragraphs.text: Espresso provides ViewActions that perform actions like clicks, typing, and scrolls on Views.

paragraphs.name: 1d67
paragraphs.text: I used perform(...) and click() to click on the Button in IntroductionActivity.

paragraphs.name: dd2d
paragraphs.text: Verifying Intents

paragraphs.name: 6ec0
paragraphs.text: To verify that the app launches the correct Intent when clicking the Button, the test has to do two things:
Capture the launched Intent

paragraphs.name: a445
paragraphs.text: Check that the Intent has the MainActivity as the component

paragraphs.name: 14cc
paragraphs.text: First, I used the Espresso-Intents extension to capture Intents. It lives in the androidx.test.espresso:espresso-intents dependency.

paragraphs.name: 0cc7
paragraphs.text: The pre-test and post-test hooks for IntroductionActivityTest

paragraphs.name: cf6a
paragraphs.text: I set up pre-test and post-test hooks using the Before and After JUnit annotations.

paragraphs.name: 0c15
paragraphs.text: The pre-test hook initialises the Intent captor to capture launched Intents.

paragraphs.name: c0e8
paragraphs.text: The post-test hook releases the Intent captor for garbage collection.

paragraphs.name: 92f6
paragraphs.text: Note: An IntentsTestRule can automate initialisation and release for each test.
But IntentsTestRule also launches the Activity under test. This conflicts with the ActivityScenarioRule that I’ve set up.

paragraphs.name: 405a
paragraphs.text: Next, I used the intended() and hasComponent() methods to verify the captured Intent.

paragraphs.name: 0d74
paragraphs.text: The test case verifies the Intent on line 7

paragraphs.name: ebc1
paragraphs.text: And there you have it! onClickButton_showsMainActivity() verifies that the app launches the MainActivity after clicking on the Button.
What’s Next?

paragraphs.name: 260d
paragraphs.text: I’ve walked through the process of writing my first UI test class for Get Hacking Android. I’ve documented common patterns like test naming schemes and file structure. I’ve introduced Espresso APIs used for handling Activities, Intents, and Views.

paragraphs.name: f18b
paragraphs.text: But that isn’t all.

paragraphs.name: 759d
paragraphs.text: Get Hacking Android uses Fragments for navigating between pages. It also performs network operations with Retrofit to fetch data from a backend.

paragraphs.name: ccf2
paragraphs.text: Possibly in another article, I’ll explain testing Fragments with FragmentTransactions within ActivityScenarios. I’ll also explain waiting on network operations with Espresso idling resources.
Note: I used FragmentTransactions instead of the new FragmentScenario API. This is because Get Hacking Android has yet to migrate to AndroidX Fragments.

paragraphs.name: e777
paragraphs.text: If you use AndroidX Fragments, you should check out FragmentScenarios instead.

paragraphs.name: 88ee
paragraphs.text: I may also explain testing authentication and user inputs using different product flavours.

paragraphs.name: 070a
paragraphs.text: Further Reading

paragraphs.name: 863c
paragraphs.text: Here are some of the articles and talks I watched before starting on Android testing:

paragraphs.name: ede5
paragraphs.text: Android Developers guide on Android testing

paragraphs.name: 04cc
paragraphs.text: Google I/O 2018 talk on writing unified tests with AndroidX Test
Google I/O 2017 talk on test-driven development on Android

paragraphs.name: 7cd9
paragraphs.text: Android Developers blog post on using different product flavours for testing

paragraphs.name: 2f2e
paragraphs.text: To end off, here’s a tweet by Guillermo Rauch
UI tests are still important though.

paragraphs.name: c4e6
paragraphs.text: Editor’s note: Zhao Wei impressed us early on with his technical know-how, his willingness to learn, and his sheer speed in getting things done. As a result, he’s contributed to myriad projects during his internship, such as developing the above Android app, creating a couple of very useful Slack bots, helping build some Swift Playgrounds notebooks for our micro:bit courses, creating demo web apps for our classes, and much more. If you’re here looking for a testimonial for Zhao Wei, and this hasn’t impressed you sufficiently, email us for more enthusiastic praise.
